title: Men and Women at Work
author: Erika Bachiochi and Ivana Greco
summary: Law professors Erika Bachiochi and Ivana Greco argue that American sex-discrimination law has drifted from its original purpose—protecting individual workers from unjust treatment—into a statistical regime that pits men and women against each other as rival classes competing for positions. They trace this drift from the early civil-rights-era focus on individual qualified workers (Phillips v. Martin Marietta, Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson) through the 1991 Civil Rights Act amendments that codified disparate-impact analysis, which pressures employers to manage gender ratios regardless of individual qualifications. The authors propose three reforms: eliminating or weakening the disparate-impact test so that all sex-discrimination claims require proof of discriminatory intent; extending USERRA-like protections to pregnant and nursing mothers who bear unique burdens in contributing to the common good through childbearing; and shifting policy focus from elite women competing in STEM to working-class women who face the most serious harassment and fewest workplace protections. They argue this framework would both reduce hostility between the sexes and better serve the women civil-rights law was originally designed to protect.
points: Reform or eliminate the disparate-impact test for sex discrimination: it creates perverse incentives for employers to manage ratios rather than evaluate individual qualifications, pitting men and women against each other.

Extend USERRA-style job protections to pregnant and nursing mothers, recognizing their socially essential contribution to the common good just as servicemembers receive special employment protections.
Redirect policy attention from elite women in STEM toward working-class women, who face disproportionate harassment, the fewest protections, and the least access to legal recourse.
Distinguish between legitimate support programs (mentoring, maternity integration) and DEI measures that constitute illegal reverse discrimination; the former deserve support, the latter do not.

Encourage employers to discuss parental leave preferences openly with employees of both sexes—these conversations are legal and humane, and flexible policies that account for the different roles of mothers and fathers serve families better.
quotes: The just goal of opening doors for individual women to have the equal opportunity to work without discrimination or abuse—once attained in Title VII and its early case law—has been traded for its inverse.
Any framework reducing a person to a class proxy will eventually fail the persons inside the class.

The law should have no quarrel with a world in which nursing or early education remain mostly women's professions, while construction or technology remain professions men prefer. Title VII's rightful goal is merely to ensure that the more unusual male nurse or female technologist can obtain and excel at his or her chosen profession.
Sexual harassment remains a serious problem in the workplace, and despite decades of effort, most cases go unreported, and most plaintiffs do not achieve relief through the courts.
The security of a mother's job may be the only financial lifeline she has.
